inputs.sbc_source: FY26 10-K/Annual Report cash flow statement 'Share-based payments' add-back, $1.2m -- SUL is an SBC-near-zero market (0.03% of revenue); kept explicit rather than zeroed
inputs.fiscal_year_end: last Saturday of June (52/53-week retail calendar; FY2016 and FY2022 were 53-week years)
inputs.price_as_of: 2026-09-25T04:58:26Z regular session, Yahoo Finance chart API
inputs.share_count_date: 2026-06-27 (FY26 Annual Report note 8(c), weighted average diluted 227.215m; CSV SharesDiluted 227.263m used)
inputs.wacc_rationale: AUD flows discounted at an AUD-built WACC: ~4.4% AU 10yr bond + ~5.5% ERP x ~1.0-1.1 beta for a discretionary multi-banner retailer, plus a modest premium for FY25-26 governance disruption (CEO dismissal, whistleblower litigation) and unproven Ignite execution risk. Base 9.5%; bull 8.5% (execution de-risked); bear 11.0% (risk also compounds in the flows via a depressed margin path -- this WACC spread reflects financing-cost/multiple risk, not a re-charge of the same operating risk already in the bear cash flows).
inputs.lease_treatment: Treatment (B) -- leases as operating cost. SUL reports via the direct cash-flow method: operating cash flow already excludes BOTH lease principal (financing activity, $252.5m FY26) and lease interest (financing activity, part of $79.1m 'Interest and borrowing costs paid'). The owner-FCF build therefore starts from the company's own published pre-AASB16 EBITDA (rental expense treated as a single opex line, $366.6m FY26; see FY26 Annual Report note 22(a) fixed-charge-cover reconciliation) rather than the post-AASB16 Segment EBITDA of $773.7m, and D&A/finance costs used are the pre-AASB16 (ex-lease) figures ($120.4m D&A, $12.8m finance costs FY26). Net debt is bank borrowings less cash only ($30.7m - $16.7m = $14.0m), matching the company's own headline 'net debt of $14 million'; the $1,291.0m of lease liabilities is deliberately excluded from net debt under this treatment to avoid double-counting the lease cost that is already charged above the FCF line.
inputs.nci_treatment: None -- no non-controlling interests; SUL is 100% owned across all four banners and both countries (AU/NZ).
inputs.notes: Model: owner-FCF component DCF (SKILL.md routing table: 'Operating company, non-US or cyclical: industrials, consumer' -> owner-fcf.md + owner-fcf-adaptations.md). SUL is a multi-banner discretionary retailer (Supercheap Auto, rebel, BCF, Macpac), non-US, AUD reporting = AUD quote (no FX adjustment needed), material AASB16 leases requiring the treatment-B adjustment above, and a genuinely cyclical/mid-cycle-normalization situation: FY26 normalised PBT fell 7% YoY on a one-off fuel-price cost shock plus ~$20m after-tax of CEO-termination/governance costs, against a newly announced (June 2026) five-year plan targeting mid-to-high single-digit normalised PBT growth to FY31 and ~$75m/yr Ignite cost savings by FY29. Historical growth CAGRs are distorted by FY21's COVID-stimulus demand spike (EBITDA peaked at $557.4m pre-AASB16 on revenue of only $3,453.1m, a 16.1% margin never repeated since) -- FY21-26 equity/EPS/FCF CAGRs are all flat-to-negative despite +4.0%/yr revenue growth, a >30% divergence flagged in historical_growth. inputs.last_fcf (208.2) is the FY26 owner FCF computed on the pre-AASB16 (Treatment B) component basis: pre-AASB16 EBITDA (454.5) - SBC (1.2) - D&A ex-lease (120.4) = EBIT (332.9), taxed at the FY26 effective rate (25.8%) per the engine convention (NOPAT = EBIT x (1-tax)) to give NOPAT 247.0, +D&A 120.4, -capex 123.4, -working-capital increase 34.3, -interest income 1.5 = 208.2. This reconciles closely to the company's own audited pre-AASB16 normalised NPAT of 236.5 (implied NPAT at the same 25.8% rate on pre-AASB16 PBT of 321.3 is 238.4, a 0.8% tie) and is materially below the reported (post-AASB16, lease-cost-excluded) FCF of 469.7 -- the ~261.5 gap is the full annual cash cost of leases (principal 252.5 + interest 69.8, net of the smaller ROI from lower ex-lease D&A/tax) that SUL's direct-method cash flow statement routes entirely through financing activities and which is therefore invisible in reported OCF/FCF. The base case underwrites revenue growth (store rollout, ~3% p.a. blended) and a PARTIAL margin recovery (roughly half of the Ignite savings ramp, margin recovering from FY26's 10.8% trough to ~12.3% by year 10, well short of the ~14%+ implied by full FY31 guidance delivery), treating full guidance delivery as bull-case upside given the still-unproven new executive team and multi-year ERP/AI transformation risk.

historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Equity/EPS/FCF 5yr CAGRs (1.2%/-7.3%/-1.8%) diverge >30% from revenue 5yr CAGR (4.0%). Cause identified, not a data error: FY2021 was a COVID-stimulus demand spike (pre-AASB16 EBITDA margin 16.1%, vs 10.8-13.6% every other year FY22-26) that inflates the FY21 starting base for every non-revenue metric. Revenue is used as the growth anchor for this reason; margin recovery is modelled explicitly and conservatively in the component build (see inputs.notes) rather than assumed via a blended CAGR.

base.narrative: Base case: FY26's fuel-shock/CODB margin trough (10.8% pre-AASB16 EBITDA margin) is the low point, not the new normal. Revenue grows ~3.5-4%/yr from continued store rollout (797 -> ~900 stores over the horizon) and modest LFL, decelerating to ~2.5% terminal as the network matures. Margin recovers gradually to ~12.3% by year 6-10 as roughly half of the guided ~$75m/yr Ignite savings flow through (net of continued cost-of-doing-business inflation and ongoing transformation spend) -- underwriting partial credibility for the new five-year plan without assuming full FY31 guidance delivery from a largely new executive team. Capex steps up to ~3.7% of revenue near-term (Truganina DC completion, Ignite systems build, new-store capex) before tapering to a steady-state ~3.0%. Working capital continues to consume cash at a moderate rate (wc_capture -20%) as inventory builds to support store growth, consistent with the FY25->FY26 trend (total working capital +$34.3m on +$129.7m revenue growth, an observed -26% capture).

bull.narrative: Bull case: the June 2026 five-year strategy is delivered largely as guided. Ignite hits close to its full ~$75m/yr run-rate savings by FY29, the new leadership team (Bradshaw plus a fully refreshed MD bench) executes the store rollout to 900+ locations without disruption, and mid-to-high single-digit normalised PBT growth is sustained through FY31 and beyond. Loyalty-program monetisation (13.1m Club members, 86% of sales) drives LFL outperformance, and margin recovers past its FY21 COVID-peak level (14%+) on a structurally lower cost base. Working capital drag is milder (-15% capture) as improved inventory management (new DC, ERP) partially offsets store-growth-driven builds.

bear.narrative: Bear case: consumer discretionary pressure (interest rates, cost-of-living, fuel-price volatility) persists well into FY27-28, and Ignite becomes a costly, multi-year distraction rather than a clean cost-out program -- the ~$30m/yr of project investment continues without the promised ~$75m of offsetting savings materialising on schedule, so margin stays pinned near or below the FY26 trough (9.8-10.3%). Competitive/structural pressure intensifies (trade partners moving direct-to-consumer, online/offline competition, BCF weather volatility, Macpac's small scale and NZ/AUD FX sensitivity). The largely-new executive bench (CEO, CFO, and most MD roles turned over within 12-18 months) struggles to execute the store rollout and ERP transformation simultaneously, and working capital drag intensifies (-28% capture) as inventory management deteriorates under transformation-program disruption.

scenario_narratives.base: Margin trough in the rear-view, partial credibility for Ignite: revenue grows with the store network and modest LFL, margin recovers about halfway from FY26's 10.8% trough toward the level implied by full guidance delivery.
scenario_narratives.bull: The new five-year strategy lands close to as-guided: ~$75m/yr Ignite savings materialise, the refreshed leadership team executes the 900+-store rollout cleanly, and margin recovers past its FY21 COVID-era peak.
scenario_narratives.bear: Consumer softness persists, Ignite is a costly distraction rather than a clean savings program, and the largely-new executive bench struggles to execute store growth and systems transformation at the same time -- margin stays pinned near the FY26 trough.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Bear weight held above the 15% house floor (25%) because the bull case requires several things to go right simultaneously from a largely unproven, newly-appointed executive team (CEO Nov-2025, CFO and most banner MDs turned over within the last 12-18 months) executing an ambitious ERP/AI transformation and a 130+ store rollout at the same time -- genuine execution risk on top of ordinary discretionary-retail cyclicality, following a governance crisis (CEO dismissal, whistleblower litigation) that itself evidences prior board-oversight weakness. Bull correspondingly trimmed to 25% since it requires full guidance delivery, not just partial recovery. Base holds the house default 50%.

valuation_philosophy.summary: Super Retail Group is valued as a mature, cyclical multi-banner specialty retailer via a component-built owner-FCF DCF (lease Treatment B: the company's own pre-AASB16, ex-lease EBITDA and D&A are used as the flow basis, since SUL's direct-method cash flow statement already fully excludes both lease principal and lease interest from operating cash flow; net debt is bank debt only, matching the company's own '$14m net debt' headline). FY26 marks a cyclical trough -- a one-off fuel-price cost shock plus ~$20m after-tax of CEO-termination and governance costs pushed normalised PBT down 7% YoY even as sales hit a record $4.2bn -- against a newly announced five-year plan (mid-to-high single-digit normalised PBT growth to FY31, ~$75m/yr Ignite cost savings by FY29, 797->900+ stores). The base case treats this as a genuine but only partially-underwritten recovery: margin recovers about halfway from the FY26 trough toward what full guidance delivery would imply, reflecting real execution risk from a largely new executive bench (CEO, CFO and most banner Managing Directors all appointed within the past 12-18 months) delivering an ambitious multi-year ERP/AI transformation and store rollout simultaneously. Full guidance delivery is treated as bull-case upside, not the central case. SBC is immaterial at SUL (0.03% of revenue) so the house/street bands are expected to sit close together despite being kept explicit rather than zeroed.
key_risks_to_valuation: Ignite transformation program fails to deliver its ~$75m/yr targeted savings on schedule, or the ~$30m/yr of project investment persists without offsetting benefit, keeping margin pinned near the FY26 trough
Consumer discretionary spending remains under sustained pressure from interest rates, cost-of-living and fuel-price volatility, suppressing like-for-like sales across all four banners

Execution risk from a largely new, unproven executive team (CEO Nov-2025, CFO and most MD roles turned over within 12-18 months) attempting a simultaneous store rollout and ERP/AI systems transformation
Recurrence of governance/conduct issues following the 2025 CEO dismissal and whistleblower litigation, which already evidenced weaknesses in board oversight

Structural competitive threats: trade partners moving to direct-to-consumer models, aggressive online/offline competition (Amazon, Kogan), and only 13% online penetration relative to more digitally mature peers
Weather/environmental volatility at BCF (algae bloom, coastal disruption) and Macpac (mild winters depressing demand), which can swing segment profit meaningfully year to year
AUD/NZD currency translation exposure via Macpac and NZ operations
